UK project Vauxhall Residences in Liverpool to launch for sale, prices from GBP195,000
article:
Vauxhall Residences, a new residential development in Liverpool, UK, will launch for sale in Singapore during the weekend of Oct 3 and 4.

The project is located in Pumpfields, an emerging district at the northern edge of Liverpool’s city centre. It offers 158 units of one- and two-bedroom apartments, along with two- and three-bedroom townhouses.

Savills Singapore is marketing the properties. According to the firm, prices for the homes start from:

GBP195,000 (about $330,000) for a one-bedder GBP 288,500 for a two-bedder GBP 280,000 for a two-bed townhouse GBP335,000 for a three-bed townhouse

The development will include amenities such as a gym, co-working space, a cafe and rooftop gardens. It is expected to be completed in 4Q2028.

It is 600m away from the Moorfields railway station and 1.3km away from Liverpool Lime Street Station, a major transportation hub with direct services to London, Manchester and other cities.

Pumpfields is a 75-acre (30ha) regeneration zone that will see the former industrial district redeveloped into a mixed-use neighbourhood with new residential, commercial and community spaces. It is part of a wider transformation of Liverpool’s historic northern docks.

The rejuvenated Pumpfields district is slated to deliver over 7,000 new homes, alongside an urban park, public squares, green corridors and improved connections to the waterfront.

Vauxhall Residences is a project by Rosmara Development Group, a Manchester-based developer.

Adrian Lim, senior director and head of international residential sales at Savills Singapore, notes that Liverpool is compelling to Singapore buyers looking at UK property.

“It is a globally recognised city with a strong cultural identity, a large student population and an established business base, while significant regeneration is creating new neighbourhoods and opportunities beyond its traditional city centre,” he explained.

Vauxhall Residences’ proximity to the Liverpool city centre, along with the ongoing rejuvenation of Pumpfields and the wider district, makes the project "particularly interesting for buyers taking a longer-term view", Lim added.

Savills will be holding a launch event for Vauxhall Residences on Oct 3 and 4 at Voco Orchard Hotel, from 2pm to 6pm.

title: Hilton brings Motto brand to Japan with 108-room Kyoto hotel opening in 2029
article:
Hilton is partnering with Heiwa Real Estate Co to open Motto by Hilton Kyoto Shijo Karasuma. The 108-key hotel will open in 2029.

This will be the first Motto by Hilton property in Japan. The hotel will include an all-day dining restaurant and a lounge with an open terrace.

“Motto by Hilton Kyoto Shijo Karasuma will offer a fresh, locally rooted hospitality experience that encourages gathering, creating a new type of stay for guests looking to immerse themselves in Japan's cultural capital,” said Alex Shockley, Hilton’ senior director, lifestyle and collection brands for Asia Pacific.

Hilton will manage the property for Heiwa. The Japanese developer and real estate company manages a portfolio of commercial and residential properties in Japan, including the stock exchange buildings in cities such as Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya and Fukuoka.

“As part of our efforts to realise our long-term vision, WAY2040, we are expanding our hotel business as a new area of growth,” said Kiyoyuki Tsuchimoto, the company’s representative executive officer, president and CEO.

The hotel will be a two-minute walk from Shijo Station on the Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line and Karasuma Station on the Hankyu Kyoto Line. This will allow guests convenient transport access to popular Kyoto attractions such as Nishiki Market, the historic Gion and Higashiyama districts, and retail offerings in the Shijo Kawaramachi area.

Hilton currently operates 13 Motto hotels, with over 24 hotels under development. Recent openings included properties in Brazil and Nashville, USA, while the group has also inked agreements for properties in Paris, Shanghai and Sydney.

In Kyoto, Hilton’s portfolio is set to grow to seven hotels across various brands, including an upcoming Curio Collection by Hilton property.

title: Do property auctions deliver bargains? Condo sales linked to money laundering case offer a mixed answer
article:
Four of 19 condo units linked to Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case sold for a combined $16.28 million at SRI’s auction on Sept 23.

All four changed hands below their opening prices. But did their buyers pay less than market value?

A comparison with resale transactions at Martin Modern and Wallich Residence suggests the answer varies by unit.

One Martin Modern apartment appears to have sold at a modest discount after allowing for floor differences. The other fetched a price close to comparable sales.

At Wallich Residence, the size of the discount depends on which past sale is used for comparison and when it took place.

For this analysis, comparable transactions were adjusted by 0.4% for each floor separating them from the auction unit. This is a working assumption within the broad 0.3%–0.5% guide we have previously used. Same-stack and same-size transactions were prioritised.

These comparisons do not account for differences in condition or renovation needs. Some buyers may also be put off by a property’s links to the money laundering case.

Table: Transacted prices at auction vs. estimated market values

Table: SRI, URA, EdgeProp Research

Martin Modern: #26-10

At Martin Modern, the strongest evidence of a discount comes from unit #26-10.

Its auction price was $39,300, or 1.8%, below its last purchase price from the developer in 2020, before stamp duties and other costs.

A unit 13 floors below it, #13-10, sold for $2.1 million in August 2026. Another apartment in the same stack, #17-10, changed hands for $2.15 million in December 2025. All three have the same floor area.

Adjusting those transactions to the 26th floor produces benchmarks of about $2.209 million and $2.227 million. Their average is $2.218 million, putting the auction result about $98,000, or 4.4%, below it.

This buyer therefore appears to have secured a relatively attractive price for the higher floor, assuming comparable condition.

Martin Modern: #17-06

The other Martin Modern sale, unit #17-06, gives a different result.

Its auction price was $63,000, or 3.1%, above its last purchase price from the developer in 2020, before stamp duties and other costs.

The closest floor comparisons are #18-06, which sold for $2.058 million in October 2025, and #15-06, which fetched $2.1 million in September 2025. Adjusted to the 17th floor, they imply values of approximately $2.050 million and $2.117 million.

Their average of $2.083 million is just $3,000 above the auction result. More recent same-stack sales support a similar reading: after floor adjustments, #11-06’s July 2026 transaction implies about $2.107 million, while #13-06’s March sale implies $2.032 million.

On this evidence, #17-06 sold broadly in line with the market. Its auction sale does not show a meaningful discount or premium.

Wallich Residence: #53-01

At Wallich Residence, #53-01 initially looks like a more substantial bargain.

The same-sized #55-01, two floors above, fetched $6.03 million in May 2025. Adjusting that price down two floors gives a benchmark of $5.982 million, against which the auction unit sold about $502,000, or 8.4%, lower.

However, that transaction preceded the auction by about 16 months. A more recent sale points to a much smaller gap. In December 2025, the 1,722 sq ft #57-08 sold for $5.7 million. Applying its psf price to #53-01’s area, then adjusting down four floors, produces a benchmark of about $5.4 million. The auction price was 1.5% higher.

The different stack could account for differences in layout and view, so this is a less direct comparable. Nevertheless, it shows why the 8.4% gap should be described as a discount to a particular earlier transaction, rather than a proven discount to current market value.

Wallich Residence: #61-02

The same issue affects #61-02 at Wallich Residence.

Using #57-08’s December 2025 transaction, adjusted for area and up four floors, gives a benchmark of about $6.696 million. The auction result was only 1.4% lower.

Using #55-01’s May 2025 sale instead produces a much higher benchmark of $7.415 million after area and floor adjustments. Against that figure, the auction price was 11% lower.

Both comparisons involve smaller apartments in different stacks. Their wide spread makes it difficult to assign a precise current-market discount to #61-02. Adjusting for floor alone cannot resolve differences in layout or the price buyers are willing to pay for a larger home.

Conclusion

The four completed sales show where buyers’ offers and sellers’ acceptance levels met. They do not establish whether the auction process itself increased or reduced the price compared with other methods of sale.

The strongest evidence of a discount among those that went under the hammer, is at Martin Modern #26-10.  The other Martin Modern unit traded close to its comparable benchmark.

Wallich Residence’s results sit nearer to the more recent resale evidence than some older transactions might suggest.

For buyers, a useful question is how an auction price compares with genuinely similar homes. For sellers, competitive bidding can improve an offer, but these four sales provide no evidence of a consistent premium from choosing an auction.

title: Leasing kicks off at One Comcentre office and retail hub, with 1ha elevated park in heart of Orchard
article:
Amid keen interest from prospective tenants, leasing has officially begun for One Comcentre — billed as the first new Grade A office and retail development in the Orchard area in two decades — ahead of its targeted completion by end-2028.

The mixed-use project is the redevelopment of Singtel's former headquarters, then known as Comcentre, in Somerset.

Richard Paine, Lendlease senior advisor, development, noted that there has been "considerable unsolicited interest" in leasing space at One Comcentre.

"Over 30 tenants, mainly office tenants, have approached us. We’re looking forward to formally engaging with them in the coming months," he said during the media briefing held at the showsuite.

Singtel and Lendlease are co-developers via a 51:49 joint venture, with Lendlease set to manage the property.

Meanwhile, Singtel will be the anchor tenant, taking up about 30% of the total space including its approximately 10,000 sq ft flagship retail store. That leaves around 70% available to other tenants.

The One Comcentre showsuite is housed at TripleOne Somerset , with views of the construction site ; interactive screens showcasing the development’s technology, sustainability and employee experience; as well as virtual AI hosts and physical AI robots.

Over 1 million sq ft of offices, amenities, public spaces

When completed, One Comcentre will comprise twin 20-storey towers, injecting more than 1 million sq ft in gross floor area (GFA) of Grade A offices, retail, dining, wellness and community spaces.

Workplaces, with large office floor plates of about 25,000 to 27,000 sq ft, will make up roughly 80% of GFA. Equipped with 5G+ connectivity, the future-ready development will be able to support AI and intelligent building operations.

The other 20% of floor space will go to six storeys of amenities, including two food courts, medical suites, fitness and wellness facilities, a 400-person auditorium for corporate events, and a private members’ club.

The aim is to create a vibrant hub that brings together workplaces, lifestyle offerings and public spaces.

One Comcentre will also feature an elevated public park or ‘Botanic Ribbon’ wrapping around the buildings from levels two to four, spanning close to 1ha. Rooftop sky gardens, accessible only to occupiers, will sit at the top floor of both towers.

The development is designed by New York-based, award-winning architecture firm Kohn Pederson Fox, while the landscape design is by Field Operations, which was the project lead for the acclaimed The High Line public park in Manhattan.

"Our desire is for One Comcentre to be the new landmark in the heart of Orchard," said Gan Siok Hoon, Singtel’s group chief corporate officer, at the media briefing.

"Just like our previous Comcentre was a very iconic building, our vision for this is also for it to be the new beacon to the future, showcasing how we can bring together technology, sustainability, and human-centered design," she added.

AI-native, future-ready building centred around sustainability

One Comcentre achieves several firsts: It is Singapore’s first AI-native building powered by dedicated 5G+ connectivity, the first end-to-end carbon-neutral commercial development in the country, and the first development in Asia to obtain triple certification in sustainability and wellbeing.

"Singtel will integrate its connectivity and AI capabilities into the development from the ground up," the co-developers said in a joint release on Sept 30.

Singtel’s 5G+ network will enable network slicing, which acts as a “priority lane” or digital expressway for occupiers. This offers high-speed, low-latency and secure communications between building systems, applications and devices.

It will mean priority network performance for cloud platforms, next-generation AI applications, physical AI such as robotics, video collaboration and other business-critical operations — even during periods of peak demand.

"As Singtel is the co-developer and anchor tenant, we will always ensure that the building infrastructure and technologies stays ahead of the curve," Gan said. "Tenants can get first access to advanced technologies without having to invest in the underlying infrastructure."

In addition, tenants can tap a suite of Singtel services, including security-as-a-service and robotics-as-a-service.

As for its sustainability credentials, One Comcentre is carbon-neutral from its design and construction to operations.

The development uses low-carbon concrete and steel to lower embodied carbon, while 90% of demolished structural materials are recovered and recycled to promote circular construction.

The result is up to 30% savings on embodied carbon, equivalent to more than 7,000 cars off the roads for a year.

One Comcentre is also the first new-build large-scale development to achieve the latest BCA Green Mark Version 7 , with a Zero Energy rating. This is in addition to the WELL Version 2 Platinum Certification and, on completion, the International Living Future Institute Zero Carbon Certification.

"These credentials support our future tenants’ ESG (environmental, social and governance) ambitions, sustainability reporting and corporate targets," said Debra Ma, Lendlease director of development, Singapore, and project director for the One Comcentre project.

Tight supply in Singapore office market

The launch comes as Singapore’s Grade A office market faces its tightest supply conditions in nearly two decades, with few major developments entering the market.

The vacancy rate of core CBD Grade A offices stood at 3.3% as of 2Q2026, while the upcoming supply through to 2030 is 37% below the 10-year historical average, according to CBRE Singapore research.

Meanwhile, high-growth sectors are anchoring demand. Tech, AI, private equity, asset management and insurance firms made up 56% of office leasing demand in the first half of this year, and CBRE foresees it increasing further.

Moray Armstrong, managing director for Singapore at CBRE, said the interest from a broad range of prospective tenants in One Comcentre, even before leasing had commenced formally, reflects pent-up demand for premium, future-ready workplace solutions.

"Increasingly, we are seeing tenants expand their search beyond the traditional CBD as they look for workplaces that help attract talent, strengthen culture and support long-term growth," he continued.

"Opportunities that bring these attributes together at scale are rare, particularly within Orchard Road."

A workplace with Orchard amenities on the doorstep

The upcoming mixed-use development’s location is expected to set it apart too.

Mark Goh, Singtel’s vice president, group property, noted: "We are at the doorstep of Orchard Road. I don’t think any of the other Grade A office buildings offer an Orchard Road address and amenities."

From a lifestyle perspective, many employees would likely want to live and work in a neighbourhood with ready access to dining, retail, wellness and entertainment options. That may also encourage collaboration and innovation, added Singtel's Gan.

Armstrong of CBRE likewise pointed out that many companies’ office location strategies are determined by employee engagement as well as talent attraction and retention.

"And that's really reliant, to a large degree, on having a workplace that's amenity-rich, has experience opportunities, and is engaging and energised," Armstrong said.

Besides, One Comcentre stands out as a new-generation workplace offering within a micromarket dominated by ageing stock. Some 93% of buildings in the Orchard Road area are at least 10 years or older, CBRE Research found.

Asked about the target retail tenant mix at One Comcentre, Paine from Lendlease shared that one of the key goals is to cater to the office workers.

“Orchard Road is a fantastic shopping street in its own right, so we’re not replicating what people can access. What we will be providing is convenience and amenity for the working population in the office towers,” Paine commented.

Reviving the forgotten Tiverton Lane with F&B, placemaking

At the same time, One Comcentre is designed to integrate with the surrounding precinct and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Orchard area.

"It's a very open development and we’re going to reinstitute Tiverton Lane, which will create a thoroughfare … with retail and placemaking. So people who live around the city centre will see this as a place for lunch or a nice evening meal, and to meet people and utilise the facilities," Paine said.

Tiverton Lane, now expunged, was a small side street off Killiney Road, running through the current One Comcentre site. It used to feature shophouses, which have since been demolished.

The developers will be restoring the forgotten laneway, with hopes for it to become a bustling marketplace.

"We are bringing Tiverton Lane back as a dedicated laneway for gastro bars, cafes and restaurants as a new F&B precinct," said Ma. "It is also a thoroughfare right to Exeter Road, which will improve the accessibility of the entire Somerset precinct."

This contrasts with the old Comcentre, a 32-storey skyscraper that served as Singtel’s headquarters for more than four decades. The building, which was vacated in 2024, mainly housed the company’s corporate offices, internal facilities and its flagship retail store.

"In the past, the old Comcentre tended to be a bit more insular," Goh said. "So when we were planning the new One Comcentre, we wanted to make it more porous."

He added that the intention is to create connections through the development, linking Killiney Road to Somerset MRT Station, and provide more amenities that the community and residents in the vicinity could enjoy, such as the elevated park.

And while One Comcentre is designed for the future, the development also celebrates the history of the former site.

"There are some familiar elements from the old Comcentre, like the rooftop space frame and the phone booths, which will get a new lease of life as art pieces throughout the new development," Gan said.

title: Painting robots and heritage buildings: Wee Hur Construction's Andy Lu on tackling complex projects
article:
A water pipe more than a metre in diameter lay beneath one of Wee Hur Construction’s project sites — except it was not where the project team had expected to find it.

"We have faced projects where huge water pipes were running through our sites," Andy Lu, CEO of Wee Hur Construction, tells EdgeProp Singapore .

For that project, the location of the pipe meant the team had to change the basement’s design and also divert the pipe at their own cost.

The episode illustrates the uncertainties that can come with projects with deep basements. Underground pipes, cables and other utility lines are difficult to predict, as they may be live or abandoned, and could also be located differently from what existing records and drawings indicate.

"In construction, we are always very mindful of things that are unknown," Lu says. "We do not always know what is below ground, since we can’t see it."

Wee Hur tries to identify and resolve potential issues as early as possible, including checking existing underground services, confirming whether they are still in use and arranging diversions where needed before construction works start.

"These have to be done upfront, and the process is sometimes very tedious," Lu notes.

He says each project adds to the experience that the company can bring to subsequent jobs, even when the building type or site conditions are different.

Building and innovating through two decades of change

Lu joined Wee Hur in 2006 as an assistant project manager, and has helmed the construction arm as CEO since 2024.

Over that period, the company has expanded from a build-only contractor into a group with businesses spanning property development, property investment, fund management and purpose-built student accommodation.

Wee Hur Construction has taken on projects including private and public housing, workers' dormitories, schools, nursing homes, commercial developments, religious buildings, conservation works, as well as additions and alterations (A&A).

Lu observes that the way construction projects are planned and built has also evolved markedly across the industry over the past two decades, with far more coordination now taking place before work begins on-site.

Project teams use 3D Building Information Modelling (BIM) and digital platforms to get a clearer picture of a building and work through design and construction requirements earlier.

"With all these technologies, we are able to recreate the model of the building, and can better visualise the end-product even before we start the construction work on-site," he says.

The company is applying these tools across its current pipeline, which span a range of building types and construction requirements.

These include the Wycombe Abbey School (Singapore) in Hougang, A&A works at the historic Teochew Building along Tank Road, and the upcoming residential and commercial development on Upper Thomson Road.

These new projects range from fitting an elevated football field, competition-standard swimming pool and theatre within one school campus, to integrating new construction with an existing heritage building.

Classrooms, sports and the arts on a school campus

Slated to open fully by September 2028, the Wycombe Abbey School on Hougang Avenue 3 broke ground this January .

It is developed by Wee Hur with joint venture partners BE Education, a UK-focused admissions consultancy firm, and premier British boarding school Wycombe Abbey.

The co-educational day school, for students aged two to 18, will come with not just classrooms but also an array of facilities to support co-curricular activities such as sports, visual and performing arts, and innovation.

"This project combines a lot of different facilities, each with its own unique challenges," Lu says.

For instance, it will feature an Olympic-sized competition pool, which means the team has to adhere to prescribed World Aquatics standards and dimensions.

"There's also an elevated football field on the second storey [in the preliminary design], as well as a full on-premise kitchen and canteen serving the whole school population. These are aspects not normally seen in a typical project," he adds.

Besides, the music rooms, dance studio and theatre require acoustic treatment to prevent sound from disrupting classes and other activities.

The theatre in particular is a sizeable auditorium with a full stage and fly bars — an overhead system used to raise and lower stage equipment such as scenery and lighting during performances.

Lu says the team also has to consider circulation within the school, including how students move between different areas.

Some of the facilities, such as the library, swimming pools and sports amenities, will also be open to the public during off-peak hours when not in use by students.

With so many uses to accommodate on the site, some are stacked across different levels.

An example is the elevated, full-sized football field that may potentially sit above the swimming pool, gym and badminton courts on the level below — a design that Lu says will "make better use of the space" available within the plot of land. The field's placement on the second storey is subject to change in the final design.

Wee Hur is bringing experience from earlier similar education-related projects to the development.

These have included building swimming pools, a sports field and basement halls for United World College of South East Asia's Dover campus, as well as an administration building and a hostel block for the Insead Asia campus in Ayer Rajah in the 2000s.

More recently, Wee Hur constructed a new 11-storey block with sports and recreational facilities at Tanglin Trust School on Portsdown Road.

Opened in early 2023, and named the Tanglin Centenary Building, the block houses a 15m climbing wall, Olympic-standard gymnastics centre, an aquatic centre with a 50m swimming pool, gym, recording studio, recital room and music rehearsal halls.

"From all these projects, we learnt the requirements and execution, and how to get them right," Lu says. "We’re using all that we've learnt to tackle challenges at the Wycombe Abbey School project as well."

Planning for multiple uses

Meanwhile, at the Upper Thomson Road mixed-use development, a basement car park will sit below a first storey containing an early childhood development centre, shops and supermarket, while residences are housed from the second storey upwards.

Wee Hur and its largest shareholder, the Goh family-controlled GSC Holdings, snagged the 262,875 sq ft site when they jointly submitted the top bid of $613.94 million in the Government Land Sale tender last October. It can yield about 595 new homes and 21,527 sq ft of commercial space.

For the group's construction arm, this means designing and planning for various typologies with diverse space requirements.

"For a residential unit, you typically have smaller spaces for the bedrooms, living room and so on, so the walls are spaced quite closely to one another. But when you go down to the supermarket, you can’t have walls every 2m," says Lu.

Each layout calls for careful planning of the building’s grid and supporting structures.

The mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems also have to be planned separately for each area, while some services are eventually combined. Wastewater discharge from various parts of the building may feed into the sewer, for example.

Clients, subcontractors and trade specialists therefore have to come on board early to "thrash out" how the design, space planning and technical systems will work together, he says.

"We have to solve very different problems at the same time and fully coordinate the requirements upfront for submission, before we can get approval to commence works on-site," Lu adds.

Giving old buildings a new lease of life

He finds conservation work especially rewarding for what can be preserved through the construction process.

"It's very meaningful because these buildings carry a lot of memory, and we are able to retain that," he says.

One of Wee Hur's ongoing A&A projects is the Teochew Building, located on the edge of River Valley. Built in 1963, the heritage property's six-storey front portion — with its distinctive Chinese roof and facade — is being conserved, while the shorter structure behind it is demolished and rebuilt.

The works include excavating a new basement carpark and reconstructing the rear portion to six storeys to match the front block.

To retain the front of the Teochew Building, Wee Hur has to protect and strengthen the existing structure, including underpinning it with piling works from within the building.

Demolishing and rebuilding the entire property would in fact be faster, easier and cheaper than conserving it.

"It's difficult, but at the end of the day, we have to make sure this heritage building is retained so that we do not lose a piece of history there," Lu notes.

Older buildings can also reveal details only after construction has started.

Original hand-sketched construction drawings may be incomplete or unavailable, while the condition and location of existing structures, pipes and other building services can become clearer after ceilings and finishes are stripped away.

Laser scanning technology helps Wee Hur capture the dimensions and existing services within such properties without relying on manual measurement and drawings.

"We can just scan it and visualise what is there very quickly," Lu shares.

Being selective with technology

Technology now plays a growing role in Wee Hur’s construction operations, although Lu is selective about which solutions the company adopts.

With a steady stream of new products entering the market, Wee Hur often meets technology vendors and solution providers to understand and keep abreast of the latest advancements.

"Sometimes it’s not easy to decide. But we stay grounded, prudent and are guided by what we actually need," Lu says.

"What problem or pain point are we trying to solve? We do not adopt for the sake of adopting. We do not want to spend money unnecessarily and do everything."

When the company identifies a potentially useful product, it trials the technology first to see whether it works as intended. Wee Hur may also provide feedback to the vendor, which Lu says can help improve the product.

Among the tools already in use are 360-degree cameras for progress tracking. A worker walks through the construction site daily with the camera to capture images, which an AI platform analyses and stitches together to give project managers and senior management a virtual view of progress.

The images can also be compared over time and against the project's BIM 3D model to check whether the completed works correspond with the design.

"This is very powerful. It enables our people to compare and take action where necessary, such as getting the subcontractor to put in more resources," Lu says.

Additionally, Wee Hur uses a cloud-based common data platform to store, communicate and share project information among developers, consultants, architects and subcontractors.

Drawings, requests for information, submissions and approvals can be handled through the platform, with each action time-stamped so that parties can easily track its status and who submitted what.

Engineers can access the same platform on tablets to refer to drawings and models and fill in digital inspection forms, which can then be signed digitally, without having to carry stacks of printed plans around.

Meanwhile, the company's AI-enabled video surveillance system flags potential safety breaches, such as if a worker standing below a load being hoisted by a tower crane, and sends the safety officer an alert and video clip for faster intervention.

In tandem, vehicle safety technology on heavy machinery, such as excavators and cranes, includes proximity sensors and cameras that warn operators and workers when people get too close.

A fatigue monitoring system also alerts operators when it detects signs of sleepiness.

Wee Hur has turned to robotics too, using it to paint the basement ceiling at the new Mount Vernon Funeral Parlour Complex project.

Lu stresses that technology and AI still need to work alongside people, as human input is needed even as more tasks are automated.

For example, with painting robots, workers still have to prepare and protect the area beforehand, operate the robot and complete any touch-ups at the areas it cannot reach.

Building capabilities for bigger, more complex projects

Looking ahead, Wee Hur is studying where technology can take its construction operations next, including reducing the industry's reliance on diesel-powered equipment.

The company is now exploring electrification as an alternative for its heavy machinery.

"All our projects are already using battery energy storage systems to cut down on diesel use and carbon emissions, and we’ve started using solar panels on the roof of the site office," Lu says.

"So the next stage is to look at whether we can use the likes of electrical excavators and electrical dump trucks."

That said, construction firms will need sufficient grid power early enough at their sites to charge the machinery, for electrification to become a viable option.

"We have surfaced these issues to the government agencies. We are working together to see how to solve this so that it makes more sense for contractors to adopt the electrification of machinery," he adds.

Strengthening Wee Hur's engineering team is another priority for Lu, who hopes a deeper talent pool will enable the contractor to take on bigger and more complex projects while maintaining its standards.

He also sees technology as one way to make construction more appealing to younger engineers, who are already accustomed to working with digital tools.

After 20 years with Wee Hur and projects spanning housing, schools, workers' accommodation and conservation, there is still one building type Lu would like to add to the construction firm's track record: a large-scale commercial development.

"We've done many types of projects, and we are always very keen on things that we have not really gone into," he says.

"Maybe it's a dream, but hopefully one day we can take on a mega commercial project."

title: REITs Underperforming in 2026 vs STI – Is It Time to Buy?
article:
2026 hasn’t been kind to Singapore
real estate investment trusts (S-REITs)
.
As at 30 September 2026, the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) had risen around 23% year-to-date, lifted by strong banking earnings.
The
iEdge S-REIT Index
(SGX: ^SREIT), meanwhile, had fallen about 12% on a price basis.
When unit prices slide faster than actual property performance, value investors naturally start looking.
Unit prices tell only half the story, though.
REITs must pay out at least 90% of taxable income to enjoy tax transparency, so distributions narrow the gap considerably over longer periods.
Looking past pure price action reveals a far more balanced total-return picture across the sector.
The key question here is: how do we separate genuine discount opportunities from classic yield traps?
Why Have Singapore REITs Lagged?
Singapore REITs lagged earlier due to persistent
higher-for-longer interest rates
.
Refinancing costs rose as older, low-cost debt matured.
At the same time, capital rotated into local banks offering stronger short-term earnings.
Weaker currencies
in the REITs’ overseas markets also squeezed distributable income.
There are signs of stabilisation, though.
All three REITs featured below grew their distribution per unit (DPU) year on year (YoY) in their latest results, supported by high occupancy and, for Keppel DC REIT and Suntec REIT, positive rental reversions.
Frasers Centrepoint Trust (SGX: J69U), or FCT – The Defensive Income Play
FCT manages an S$8.4 billion portfolio of nine heartland malls, including Causeway Point, NEX, and Northpoint City.
Essential services drive roughly 55% of gross rental income, insulating cash flows against economic slowdowns.
Operational execution remains strong, with committed retail occupancy at 99.6% as at 30 June 2026, alongside YoY gains in the first nine months of FY2026 (9MFY2026) shopper traffic (+2.0%) and tenant sales (+1.8%).
Its balance sheet is healthy.
Aggregate leverage was 40.4% as at 30 June 2026, and the proposed sale of White Sands would reduce it to about 36.5% on a pro forma basis (based on 31 March 2026 figures).
FCT has no debt left to refinance in FY2026, and its average cost of debt fell to 3.0% in 3QFY2026.
Payouts remain steady, with a 1HFY2026 DPU of S$0.06136.
At S$2.07 per unit (as at 30 September 2026), FCT provides a trailing distribution yield of 5.8%.
Upgrades at Hougang Mall and NEX, plus a 50% stake in the retail component of the new Bayshore Drive development, give FCT several sources of growth.
When market noise depresses prices for a trust running near-perfect occupancy, defensive income investors get a rare opportunity to lock in yield on the cheap.
Keppel DC REIT (SGX: AJBU) – The Growth REIT
Backed by its sponsor,
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4), Keppel DC REIT offers pure-play exposure to data centres.
Its weighted average lease expiry (WALE) is 6.7 years by lettable area and 4.5 years by rental income, since more of its income comes from colocation contracts, which tend to be shorter.
Operating demand remains robust, with contracted power capacity at about 95% and positive rental reversions of around 10% on 1H2026 contract renewals.
Portfolio occupancy dipped to 92.5% after a contract expired at Cardiff Data Centre.
Capital management remains prudent, with aggregate leverage at 34.0%, S$673 million in debt headroom, and a 2.6% average debt cost, with 87% of borrowings on fixed rates.
Driven by organic growth and acquisitions, 1H2026 DPU rose 11.3% YoY to S$0.05714.
At S$2.12 per unit (as at 30 September 2026), the REIT offers an annualised yield of 5.4%.
This strong execution was bolstered by accretive acquisitions of Tokyo Data Centre 3 and the remaining stakes in Keppel DC Singapore 3 & 4.
Suntec REIT (SGX: T82U) – The High-Yield Opportunity
Suntec REIT offers a high-yield commercial play anchored by Suntec City and Marina Bay Financial Centre.
Distributable income rose 25.5% YoY to S$116.5 million in 1H2026, and DPU climbed 24.8% to S$0.03936.
The manager credited stronger Singapore office and retail performance, lower financing costs and a smaller Australian withholding-tax provision.
It expects full-year rental reversions of close to 10% at Suntec City Mall and near 5% for its Singapore offices.
At S$1.34 per unit (as at 30 September 2026), Suntec REIT’s annualised 1H2026 DPU gives a distribution yield of about 5.9%.
Despite the stronger results, the market appears wary of Suntec REIT’s balance sheet.
Aggregate leverage rose to 43% as at 30 June 2026, from 41.5% at end-2025.
The all-in financing cost did ease to 3.55%, but with leverage this high, there is less room to absorb higher rates when debt is refinanced.
The drag from overseas holdings isn’t disappearing overnight.
Office vacancy in London’s City and West End is around 7% to 8%, and the Melbourne and Adelaide office markets remain tenant-led, although Suntec REIT expects its Australian portfolio to stay stable.
Suntec REIT’s distribution coverage now rests heavily on its Singapore assets and on capital recycling.
With Suntec REIT yielding almost 6%, investors face a clear choice: buy into a genuine valuation discount, or stay clear of a yield trap constrained by balance sheet friction.
Are Singapore REITs Cheap Now?
Valuation metrics hint that Singapore REITs trade at historically steep discounts.
SGX Research’s 2Q2026 S-REIT chartbook put the sector’s aggregate price-to-book (P/B) ratio at 0.77x as at 30 June 2026, below its 10-year average of 1.0x.
A P/B below 1.0x means units are priced below the book value of the REITs’ assets.
The average distribution yield was 6.3%, about 384 basis points above the 10-year Singapore Government Securities (SGS) yield at the time.
That price tag, however, is grounded in reality.
Refinancing at higher rates keeps squeezing profit margins, while downward revaluations of overseas offices hit balance sheets directly.
Key Drivers of the S-REIT Outlook
The S-REIT outlook comes down to a simple balance between interest rate relief and underlying property performance.
A sustained recovery needs central bank rate cuts.
Lower borrowing costs ease refinancing pressure, narrow yield spreads, and stabilise property valuations.
On the ground, Singapore retail and office assets must keep securing positive rental reversions to drive DPU growth.
Ultimately, a lasting recovery needs both lower debt costs and rising payouts.
If interest rates stay high, maturing debt will have to be refinanced at higher costs.
That would shrink distributable income and leave less buffer for payouts.
Squeezed balance sheets could even force weaker trusts to issue lower-priced units, diluting existing unitholders’ distributions.
Sector pressure will remain until these debt and operational drags clear.
Get Smart: Underperformance Can Create Opportunity, But Don’t Buy Blindly
Lagging the STI in 2026 doesn’t automatically make Singapore REITs a bargain.
Investors should figure out which ones are just wrestling with short-term interest-rate issues, and which have bigger problems, such as poor assets or dividends they can’t support.
What’s tried and tested is this: Stick to trusts that own solid assets, show strong occupancy, and keep delivering consistent DPU growth, whatever sector they are in.

title: 3 Singapore Stocks Quietly Profiting From The AI Boom
article:
The most compelling semiconductor plays tend to be
global names
such as
NVIDIA Corporation
(NASDAQ: NVDA) and
Micron Technology, Inc.
(NASDAQ: MU).
While Singapore does not mint such global tech giants, the small city-state still holds its own, being home to precision engineering and technology companies that play crucial roles in the global
semiconductor supply chain
.
Instead of designing artificial intelligence (AI) chips or building frontier language models, these AI enablers supply specialised testing equipment, precision front-end equipment components, and essential consumable tools for global chipmakers.
To sweeten the deal for local investors, these companies –
AEM Holdings Ltd.
(SGX: AWX),
UMS Integration Limited
(SGX: 558), and
Micro-Mechanics (Holdings) Ltd.
(SGX: 5DD) – pay tax-free dividends on top of potential capital appreciation.
AEM Holdings: Testing the Next Generation of AI Chips
AI processors are becoming more powerful.
But that power comes with a hefty operational cost: extreme heat generation.
While the complex designs of AI chips make them powerful, they also make them vulnerable to this intense heat.
Given this vulnerability, stress testing of costly AI chips under real-world operating conditions is more crucial than ever.
To this end, AEM’s PiXL technology fills the thermal integrity gap, offering precise thermal testing at scale to ensure high-powered AI chips can perform reliably under extreme conditions.
Strategically, it expands with a “Razor/Razorblade” model that generates recurring sales.
Crucially, analysts believe the
collaboration
between
Intel Corporation
(NASDAQ: INTC) and NVIDIA could lift demand for AEM’s testing solutions, though the benefit may only show up in the medium term.
Management has raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to between S$630 million to S$680 million, up from between S$550 million to S$600 million.
AEM’s group revenue for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) climbed 29.9% year on year (YoY) to S$247.2 million, while its net profit rose 875.6% YoY to S$30.8 million, driven by higher demand from its fabless AI/HPC customer.
Furthermore, the group’s partnership with
ASE Technology
(NYSE: ASX), a major outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider, could help AEM tap demand from hyperscalers.
With a net cash position of S$56.6 million and a low debt-to-equity ratio of 0.05x, AEM’s strong balance sheet supports a 1H2026 interim dividend of S$0.024 per share, following a final dividend of S$0.013 per share for FY2025.
UMS Integration: The Front-End Precision Powerhouse
While AEM anchors the growth in back-end AI testing, UMS offers a front-end equipment play.
UMS has long provided precision component manufacturing and electromechanical assembly for front-end chipmaking equipment to
Applied Materials
(NASDAQ: AMAT), one of the world’s largest semiconductor equipment makers and its key customer.
Crucially, UMS has also onboarded another major semiconductor equipment maker as a customer, which is starting to reduce its reliance on a single client.
In the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026), UMS’s revenue jumped 29% YoY to S$87.1 million, driving net profit up 90% to S$19.8 million, as initial contributions from this new customer ramped up, alongside increased contributions from existing customers and aerospace demand.
Notably, the company operates with net cash of S$38.6 million on its balance sheet as at 30 June 2026, with no bank borrowings, and declared a 2Q2026 interim dividend of S$0.010 per share, unchanged YoY.
Micro-Mechanics: The High-Margin Consumable Cash Machine
AI-linked equipment makers potentially face inconsistent revenue due to customers’ lumpy investment cycles.
Micro-Mechanics is less exposed to these swings.
Instead of selling costly one-off equipment, it provides high-precision, miniature consumable tools, such as die-attach and wire-bonding tools, that eventually wear out as chips are assembled and tested, sustaining recurring demand.
As global chip production rises, so does demand for these high-precision, complementary tools, which benefits Micro-Mechanics.
Additionally, by serving over 600 global customers through its localised manufacturing facilities, the company is cushioned against geopolitical friction.
In the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), Micro-Mechanics’ revenue rose 15.8% to S$75.5 million on strong demand for its consumable tools, while operating cash flow edged up 3.5% to S$18.9 million.
To sweeten the deal for investors, the company has no debt, boasts a net cash position of S$30.1 million, and rewards shareholders with a total dividend of S$0.06 per share (unchanged YoY).
This includes a proposed S$0.03 final dividend, subject to shareholder approval at its annual general meeting on 26 October 2026.
Get Smart: Riding the AI Boom with Local Names
Here’s the thing about riding the
AI boom
: You don’t necessarily need to chase expensive US tech giants.
Local AI enablers like AEM, UMS, and Micro-Mechanics offer a way to gain exposure to three parts of the AI chip supply chain: testing, front-end manufacturing and consumable tools.
Beyond growing market demand, this AI-enabling trio boasts solid balance sheets and robust profitability.
Crucially, all three pay tax-free dividends, adding a stream of income for Singapore investors on top of any business growth.

title: Get Smart: I’ll Wait For The Market To Fall Before I Buy
article:
“I’ll wait for the market to fall before I buy.”
I have heard some version of this countless times over the years.
And on the surface, it sounds perfectly sensible.
Why buy when stocks are expensive if you can wait for a better price?
Well, on 15 September 2026 (Tuesday), investors got their better price.
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) fell 79.38 points, or 1.4%, in a single day, closing at 5,638.64.
Just a day earlier, it had closed at 5,718.02.
So let me ask you a question.
Did you buy?
There was your lower price
Imagine you had S$10,000 sitting in cash on Monday.
You looked at the market and decided:
“Too expensive. I’ll wait for a pullback.”
Twenty-four hours later, the STI was almost 80 points lower.
There was your pullback.
There was your cheaper price.
Yet I suspect many investors would have found it much harder to press the buy button on Tuesday than they imagined.
Because once prices start falling, a different set of questions takes over.
What if the market falls another 100 points tomorrow?
What if this is the start of something bigger?
Maybe I should wait and see.
Perhaps it will be even cheaper next week.
And just like that, the goalposts move.
We want lower prices. But we also want certainty.
That is one of the strange things about investing.
When share prices are rising, we wish we had bought earlier.
We tell ourselves that if only prices came down a little, we would happily buy.
Then prices actually fall.
And suddenly, what we really want is not just a lower price.
We want a lower price together with reassurance that it will not fall further.
Unfortunately, markets do not usually give us both.
Lower prices rarely arrive with a note saying:
Don’t worry. Everything is fine. This is definitely a good time to buy.
Usually, they arrive together with a reason to feel nervous.
On that Tuesday, weakness across Asian markets came amid concerns over the pace of artificial intelligence development.
In Singapore, losers heavily outnumbered gainers, and all three local banks ended the day lower.
In other words, there was a reason investors felt uncomfortable.
There almost always is.
So should you have bought on Tuesday?
Here is where things get tricky.
I am not saying Tuesday was “the bottom”.
Nobody knew that.
And nobody knew whether the market would fall another 1%, 5% or 20%.
That is not the lesson.
The lesson is this:
If your plan is to wait until lower prices also feel comfortable, you may end up waiting a very long time.
By Friday, 18 September, the STI had recovered part of Tuesday’s decline.
That does not prove Tuesday was some wonderful buying opportunity. It simply shows how quickly the situation can change.
At the start of the week, the market may have looked too expensive to buy. Once prices fell, the uncertainty made buying feel uncomfortable for a different reason. And when the market recovered some ground, the hesitation simply shifted again.
That is the difficulty with waiting for the “right” moment. The reason for not buying can change faster than the market itself.
Decide before the scary day arrives
This is why I think investors should spend less time trying to predict exactly when the next correction will happen.
Instead, decide what you will do when it does.
Suppose you have S$10,000 to invest.
Maybe you do not need to put all S$10,000 into the market at once.
You could invest part of it today.
Keep some aside.
And if attractive companies become cheaper, you already know what you are prepared to do.
The exact method matters less than having a plan.
Because making calm decisions is easy when everything is calm.
The real test comes when the market falls and every headline gives you another reason to wait.
Get Smart: What will you actually do?
There will be bigger declines than last Tuesday’s.
Much bigger ones.
Some will recover quickly.
Others will not.
We will not know which is which beforehand.
So perhaps the question is not:
“When will the market give me a good opportunity to buy?”
A better question is:
“What will I actually do when it does?”
Because saying you want lower prices is easy.
Buying when lower prices finally arrive is much harder.

title: Unlocking CICT’s Growth Engine: From AEIs to a S$1.1B Hougang Expansion
article:
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, is reshaping its portfolio.
Paragon, a freehold retail and medical asset on Orchard Road, joined the
REIT
on 1 July 2026.
Asia Square Tower 2 has left the REIT’s portfolio.
Further down the line, CICT’s S$1.1 billion commercial development at Hougang Central could add another major source of income.
How did CICT fare in the first half of 2026?
Two engines drove CICT’s distribution growth in the first half of 2026 (1H 2026): full ownership of CapitaSpring and Gallileo’s handover to the European Central Bank.
Gross revenue rose 7.5% year on year to S$846.8 million.
Net property income (NPI) grew 8.7% to S$630.5 million.
Distributable income climbed 13.3% to S$466.7 million.
Distribution per unit
(DPU) increased 7.1% to S$0.0602 for 1H 2026.
Retail was the softer side.
Retail gross revenue fell 3.9% and retail NPI slipped 3.7%, largely because CICT divested Bukit Panjang Plaza in February 2026.
Tenant sales per square foot grew 1.6% and shopper traffic rose 2.4%.
Meanwhile, office rental reversion reached 6.5% in 1H 2026, up from 4.8% a year earlier.
Retail reversion eased to 4% from 7.7%.
How does the Paragon and Asia Square Tower 2 swap work?
CICT completed its Paragon acquisition on 1 July 2026.
The deal carries an agreed property value of S$3.9 billion and an overall net yield of 3.9%.
Paragon starts contributing to CICT’s income from the third quarter of 2026 (3Q 2026).
Asia Square Tower 2 headed the other way.
The divestment was completed on 17 September 2026 at an exit yield of 3%.
The sale is expected to bring in about S$2.45 billion of net proceeds.
What about debt?
CICT’s aggregate leverage stood at 37.4% on 30 June 2026.
The cost of debt fell to 2.9% from 3.4% a year ago.
Interest cover
rose to 3.9 times from 3.3 times.
Fixed-rate borrowings made up 78% of total debt, down from 81%.
Which asset enhancement projects come next?
CICT has five asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs) lined up through to 2028.
Tampines Mall comes first.
The mall’s AEI completes in 3Q 2026 at a cost of about S$24 million, with a targeted return on investment (ROI) of about 7%.
Next, CICT expects its Raffles City Tower upgrading to finish in 4Q 2026.
Lot One Shoppers’ Mall follows in 1Q 2027, with about S$37 million of capital expenditure and a targeted ROI above 7%.
Two projects are due to start in 3Q 2026.
Capital Tower’s AEI costs about S$25 million and should be completed in 4Q 2027.
The second is also the biggest AEI.
It covers Plaza Singapura and The Atrium@Orchard.
CICT plans to spend about S$160 million there for a targeted ROI of 6% to 7%, with completion in 4Q 2028.
What could Hougang Central add?
Hougang Central’s commercial component will offer about 300,000 square feet of net lettable area.
CICT puts the development cost at about S$1.1 billion.
Based on the valuer’s estimated net income, the yield on cost should exceed 5%.
The project sits in the design and planning stage.
Construction should begin in 2027, subject to planning approvals, with completion in 2030 or 2031.
Management expects no DPU impact during the development period.
Once complete, Hougang Central could give CICT’s DPU another major boost.
What risks should unitholders watch?
Paragon’s lease expiries stand out.
Retail leases making up 30.6% of Paragon’s gross rental income expire in 2027.
That is a large slug of space to re-let in a single year.
Those renewals will largely decide whether Paragon grows income beyond the 1.7% accretion that management has modelled.
The Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link poses a second risk for retail.
Its impact is anyone’s guess, but investors cannot assume there will be none, especially for malls in the west of Singapore.
Get Smart: Follow the DPU, not the deals
Asset swaps and AEIs make big headlines.
For unitholders, the real test is whether the REIT can lift its DPU over time.
With CICT, watch where aggregate leverage settles now that the Asia Square Tower 2 sale is complete.
Then track the rents Paragon secures as its 2027 leases come up for renewal.
If both head in the right direction, the AEI pipeline and Hougang Central give CICT a path to growing DPU into the next decade.

title: US mortgage rates rise to almost three-year high of 7.3%
article:
(Sept 30): US mortgage rates climbed for a sixth straight week to an almost three-year high, thwarting would-be homebuyers.

The contract rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage rose 18 basis points in the week ended Sept 25 to 7.30%, the highest since November 2023, according to Mortgage Bankers Association figures released Wednesday. The rate on a five-year adjustable mortgage surged 37 basis points to 6.47% — the highest in more than two years.

Higher home-financing costs are spelling more difficulty for an already troubled housing market. The MBA purchase index, which measures loan applications, fell 4.3% to the lowest level since April 2025. The group’s refinance gauge tumbled another 8.7%, extending a skid dating back to mid-August.

Mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury note yields, which have been climbing as conflict in the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine war keep energy costs and overall inflation elevated. On Tuesday, the 10-year yield hit the highest level in more than 19 years.

Concerns about government debt and recent data showing solid economic activity are also contributing to the rise in borrowing costs. The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate earlier this month for the first time since 2023 in an effort to tame inflation. Investors expect US central bankers will hike again by the end of the year.

Mortgage rates above 7% will keep more people tethered to their current homes because the gap between homeowners’ existing 3% or 4% mortgages and today’s higher rates is getting wider, said Mark Fleming, chief economist at title insurer First American Financial Corp.

See also: US 30-year Treasury yield rises to highest level since 2002

While sales could slow further, a large price drop is unlikely, provided there isn’t a major economic downturn that causes forced sales like foreclosures, he said.

Prices are “downside sticky,” Fleming said. “They generally slow down or stop going up.”

Sales of previously owned homes, which make up the bulk of the US housing market, have struggled to gain any traction. Contract closings fell in August to their weakest pace in more than a year.

See also: US consumer confidence plunges to lowest level since 2014

The MBA survey, which has been conducted weekly since 1990, uses responses from mortgage bankers, commercial banks and thrifts. The data cover more than 75% of all retail residential mortgage applications in the US.

title: BMW plans margin rebuild with simpler line-up and pricier cars
article:
(Sept 30): BMW AG plans to restore margins by simplifying its business, cutting costs and selling more expensive cars, according to analysts who took part in the company’s capital markets day.

The German automaker is trying to rebuild profitability after China’s ongoing price war, heavy spending on its electric-car overhaul and geopolitical upheaval squeezed returns. Management is aiming to lift auto margins to 3% to 5% by 2028 and to its long-term target range of 8% to 10% early next decade, Bernstein analyst Stephen Reitman wrote on Wednesday in a note.

Executives briefed analysts and investors on Tuesday and will publish the updated financial goals later on Wednesday, the second and final day of the capital markets day in Munich.

“BMW has a pragmatic answer to the very volatile conditions,” Ingo Speich, the head of sustainability and corporate governance at Deka Investment, said by email. “Even BMW is not immune to the changes in the industry, even if it seemed that way for a long time.”

The shares rose as much as 3.5% in Frankfurt. They are down about 40% this year, more than twice as much as the wider EURO STOXX Automobiles & Parts Index.

BMW had until recently stood out as the most resilient of Germany’s car manufacturers, helped by a flexible electric-vehicle strategy and a premium-heavy line-up. That distinction vanished with a major profit warning in June, as China’s deepening slump, fierce local competition and the huge cost of electrification hammered margins.

See also: McLaren reveals a new visual identity for automotive and racing

BMW and its European peers are facing stiff competition from upstart Chinese manufacturers at home, while also suffering steep declines in sales in China, the world’s biggest market. That has deprived them of a lucrative revenue stream they relied on for years.

The challenge for Milan Nedeljkovic, the new chief executive officer, is to claw back returns while still funding the technology and new models it needs to stay competitive. Among his first steps after taking over in May was cutting jobs by around 8,000, just over 5% of its workforce.

“BMW’s financial message is that 2026 is a transition year, with profitability expected to recover in stages,” Reitman wrote. Bernstein rates BMW as 'outperform' with a target price of EUR82 ($119). The shares closed at EUR54.50 on Tuesday.

See also: Denza B5 Zenith arrives in Singapore

The first leg of the firm’s recovery is simplification. BMW wants to pare back an offering it concedes has become too complex, shorten development times and deepen supplier partnerships.

In China, it is also shrinking its dealer network and sourcing more standardized local components, which could cut the cost of those parts by 20% to 30%, Bernstein said, citing chief financial officer Walter Mertl.

“Lowering expectations for China was the right but also inevitable path,” said Speich at Deka, which is a BMW shareholder.

The company’s plans for higher returns via cost-cutting risk falling short as the sector goes through a fundamental shift, according to Citigroup analysts.

“Investor sentiment is clearly concerned with a much more structural industry deterioration, which would in turn require a much more structural BMW response,” they wrote. Citi has a 'neutral' rating on BMW with a target price of EUR64.

The Munich-based firm is betting that more expensive, higher-margin models can help lift profits. It’s planning a new sport utility vehicle above the X7, its current flagship in the segment, more high-performance M cars and a bigger role for Alpina, the marque it is positioning between its mainstream luxury range and Rolls-Royce.

Its new generation of electric cars is another pillar of the recovery, with European orders for the iX3 already topping 100,000, Bernstein said.

title: Singapore sees first data breach linked to AI use, ST reports
article:
(Sept 30): Singapore received its first notification of an AI-related data breach after a food company accidentally disclosed customers’ email addresses to other recipients of a bulk email, the Straits Times reported, citing the country’s Personal Data Protection Commission.

Bee Cheng Hiang, a well-known local producer of Chinese-style pork jerky, told the commission that the incident occurred in April after an employee used a generative AI tool to create a programme for sending emails in batches to a local mailing list. The employee, however, failed to instruct the programme to hide each recipient’s email address from other customers. It was the first time the company had used an AI tool in its business operations, the newspaper reported on Wednesday.

The breach, which was reported to the commission two days after the incident, exposed the email addresses of more than 95,000 customers. No other personal data was affected, and the exposed information was not managed, processed or generated by any AI-powered operation or process, the commission told the Straits Times.

Bee Cheng Hiang has since introduced a requirement for at least two staff members to verify all bulk email communications before they are sent, the newspaper reported.

title: Foreign money flees India again as oil spike undoes policy gains
article:
(Sept 30): Overseas investors are turning sellers of Indian assets again as surging oil prices and rising global yields threaten to derail a recent revival in demand.

Global funds have sold US$2.1 billion of local equities so far this month, following two straight months of purchases. Outflows from index-eligible sovereign bonds are also picking up, with foreigners selling US$1.1 billion this month — on track for the biggest outflow since March — after record inflows in June. The rupee is among Asia’s worst performers this quarter despite robust inflows from a special dollar deposit programme while the 10-year government bond yield hit a two-year high this week.

The renewed selling is snuffing out a nascent recovery in foreign demand following an unprecedented stretch of underperformance by Indian stocks against regional peers. Resurgent oil prices are weighing on the rupee and stoking inflation in an economy heavily reliant on imports, leaving policymakers with limited scope to cushion markets despite a series of earlier measures to attract foreign capital.

“Oil will be the biggest factor determining whether India sees renewed foreign outflows,” said Gautam Chhaochharia, head of global markets India at UBS Group AG. The bank expects Indian stocks to remain range-bound in the near term, with valuations, share supply and high oil prices likely to limit the scope for gains.

On Wednesday, the benchmark NSE Nifty 50 Index closed at a six-month low as foreign outflows continued. Global funds sold a net 100 billion rupees of shares on Tuesday, according to provisional data, which, if confirmed, would mark the biggest withdrawal since late May.

See also: Coca-Cola is said to consider December filing for India unit’s US$1 bil IPO

The retreat by global funds is not confined to India, with markets from Korea to Taiwan also seeing outflows after attracting money in August. The reversal in the South Asian nation follows an improvement in foreign demand earlier in the quarter. Despite September’s selling, overseas funds have bought a net of US$2.7 billion of Indian shares since July, putting the country on track for its first quarterly inflow since April-June last year.

Policymakers have also taken steps to support the rupee. Banks garnered US$133 billion from a special diaspora programme. The dollars have been swapped with the Reserve Bank of India, which briefly pushed up reserves to a record US$785.7 billion. Still, the central bank has been selling dollars to support the rupee as elevated energy prices weigh on the currency.

“The recent foreign selling should be viewed primarily in the context of the broader global bond-market correction, rather than as a fundamental reassessment of India,” said Fesa Wibawa, investment manager of fixed income Asia at Aberdeen Investments. The pullback offers an opportunity to gradually increase exposure, he said.

See also: Delhi moves early with pollution curbs to fight winter smog

Even so, higher global yields are making it hard for India to attract overseas capital as investors pull away from most emerging markets. Foreign funds have yanked more than US$45 billion from Indian stocks since the end of 2024, partly as money flowed toward northern Asian markets with exposure to the artificial intelligence trade.

The higher returns available on Treasuries are particularly relevant for India because US-based investors account for the largest pool of foreign portfolio equity assets. Rupee weakness and the cost of hedging against further declines also erode dollar returns on Indian assets. Meanwhile, rising bets on interest-rate hikes by the central bank are adding to unease over the growth outlook for both bond and stock investors.

Equity valuations add to the challenge. MSCI Inc’s broader gauge of Indian equities still trades a premium to Asian equities despite heading for its worst year since 2011. Earnings for the 160-plus member gauge are expected to climb 13% in 2027, the slowest among major peers including China, South Korea and Taiwan. With developed-market yields elevated, investors are demanding stronger earnings growth to justify that premium.

“Though India’s macro buffers have increased with FCNR flows, capital-flight risks have also risen with rate hikes in developed markets,” Kunal Vohra, strategist at BNP Paribas SA, wrote in a note this week. “Rising oil prices and commodity inflation remain a material challenge for India in the near term.”

title: Coca-Cola is said to consider December filing for India unit’s US$1 bil IPO
article:
(Sept 30): Coca-Cola Co is considering filing a draft prospectus in December for an initial public offering of its Indian bottling unit, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Atlanta-based drinks giant has also added Axis Capital Ltd and IIFL Capital Services Ltd to the roster of banks working on the Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages Pvt deal, the people said, asking not to be identified because the deliberations are private.

The IPO is expected to consist largely of shares sold by existing investors, with Coca-Cola seeking a valuation of about US$10 billion, the people said. Bloomberg News has reported previously that the IPO could raise around US$1 billion.

Deliberations are ongoing, so details including the timing, valuation and structure of the offering may change. Representatives for Coca-Cola and the banks did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Coca-Cola is also working with Kotak Mahindra Capital Co, Citigroup Inc, JPMorgan Chase & Co and Morgan Stanley on the IPO, local media has reported.

A listing would help Coca-Cola tap strong investor demand for new offerings in India while unlocking value from one of the country’s largest bottling operations. Proceeds from IPOs in India have reached almost US$10 billion in July-September — the most ever for the quarter — thanks to blockbuster offerings by the National Stock Exchange of India Ltd and SBI Funds Management Ltd. The country is now on track for one of its best years ever, with over US$13 billion raised already in nearly 250 IPOs, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

See also: Delhi moves early with pollution curbs to fight winter smog

title: Dollar enjoys best month since June on Fed’s inflation fight
article:
(Sept 30): The dollar is wrapping up its best month since June after the Federal Reserve’s renewed focus on taming inflation pushed interest-rate expectations and US bond yields higher.

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index has risen 1.8% in September, touching the highest level in two months. Solid US economic data and heightened inflation risks have been lifting the currency. The war in Iran has kept energy prices elevated and pushed Treasury yields to historical peaks, with the 30-year reaching the highest level since 2002.

The market is now pricing in nearly one percentage point of Fed rate increases in the next 12 months, further strengthening the greenback.

“The dollar has continued to take its cue from US data,” said Jayati Bharadwaj, head of foreign-exchange strategy at TD Securities. “US data surprises are the directional signal for the dollar in the near term and whether the Fed can hike close to how much the markets are priced for.”

The rally that followed the Fed’s first rate hike in three years continues to be fuelled by policymakers’ hawkish remarks. Fed Governor Michael Barr on Tuesday reiterated his warning that more rate increases will likely be needed to slow inflation. Similarly, New York Fed President John Williams said one more rate hike “may be appropriate late this year to support a timelier return of inflation to target”.

See also: Yen strengthens past 157 per dollar, outperforming G-10 peers

Widening interest-rate differentials and robust US economic growth are also forcing dollar bears to rethink their positions. Morgan Stanley recently abandoned its long-held view that the dollar will weaken in the second half of 2026.

Traders are now closely watching the September jobs report set for this Friday, which will test aggressive monetary tightening bets. The US is also scheduled to release the personal consumption expenditures price index for August, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, on Wednesday.

Inflation risks are elevated across the globe but not all economies are positioned to withstand more aggressive rate increases. The expectation of the rates-path differentials is guiding the dollar outlook against its peers.

See also: Dollar’s best rally since March has legs as fortunes shift

All Group-of-10 currencies except the yen have weakened against the dollar in September. The rising risks of Japanese authorities stepping into the foreign-exchange market and expectations of more rate hikes from the Bank of Japan are supporting the yen.

Options pricing shows traders favour the greenback across tenors. So-called risk reversals, a measure of bullish versus bearish demand, are near their strongest pro-dollar levels since June.

However, some indicators suggest the dollar’s run may be tiring. A measure of the greenback’s momentum climbed above 70 on Tuesday, indicating it might be overbought. On Sept 24, Bloomberg’s relative strength index for the dollar had reached overvalued territory as well.

“We think the dollar is beginning to look stretched,” said Noah Buffam, strategist at CIBC Capital Markets.

Kamakshya Trivedi, global head of foreign exchange and interest rate forecasts at Goldman Sachs Group Inc, expects the dollar to trade within its current range, predicting the Fed will only raise rates one more time in October.

title: DFI to pocket US$340 mil exchanging assets with long time F&B partner
article:
DFI Retail Group will pocket cash proceeds of some US$340 million selling its interests in the Maxim's branded chain of food and beverage outlets to its longtime joint venture partner.

Under a 50-50 joint venture dating back some four decades, Jardine, the parent company of DFI Retail, and Hong Kong Caterers, owned by the Wu family, run a Hong Kong-based F&B empire that also consists of the Starbucks regional franchise in seven Asian markets including Singapore.

As part of this "reorganisation", DFI Retail will assume full control over some 1,100 Starbucks outlets that is now part of the joint venture.

"The reorganisation will mark the final milestone of the group’s pivot from a portfolio company to a focused operating company," reads DFI's announcement.

The US$340 million which DFI will receive from the Wu family is the difference in the value of these two groups of assets.

DFI plans to apply the proceeds to pursue M&A, and to also return excess capital to shareholders. It plans to improve its dividend payout ratio to 80% in 2027, up from 70% now.

See also: PLUS points: What’s in CDL’s three-year roadmap?

According to DFI, the Starbucks licensed business in 2025 generated revenue of close to US$750 million with an underlying operating margin of 7%. Revenue grew at a 3.5% cumulative annual growth rate (CAGR) from 2023 to 2025.

DFI says that upon completion, the Starbucks licensed business will be immediately revenue and operating margin accretive to its core retail business, with further upside from operating synergies.

Specifically, the Starbucks licensed business is expected to contribute US$600-650 million to DFI’s total subsidiaries’ revenue from April to December 2027, and around US$900 million on a full-year basis in 2028

See also: CDL shares swoon to six-week low after $6 bil divestment target news

DFI aims to generate 6-7% revenue CAGR from 2026 to 2029. This will be supported by an expanding coffeehouse footprint to at least 1,350 locations alongside improved store sales density.

The company is aiming for a mid-term operating margin of 8-9% and realise an estimated US$10 million in operating synergies in the first full year post-consolidation across procurement, overhead and real estate optimisation, among other areas.

DFI Retail Group shares closed at US$3.19 on Sept 30, down 1.54% for the day, extending a loss of 18.83% year to date.

title: Singapore, Malaysia cloaked in haze before key sports events
article:
(Sept 30): Singapore and Kuala Lumpur are choking under severe haze spewing from wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia, with air quality deteriorating dramatically ahead of major sporting events.

The two cities currently rank among the top five most polluted in the world, according to data compiled by IQAir. Forecasts show that the conditions driving the latest haze episode, including widespread dryness and prevailing east-to-southeast winds, are expected to persist for another week.

Malaysia is due to host its first Formula One race in nine years this weekend at the Sepang International Circuit, alongside the Standard Chartered Marathon in Kuala Lumpur, and the acrid conditions could disrupt both events. Organisers of the long-distance running race said they are weighing contingency plans should conditions deteriorate. Le Tour de Langkawi, a multi-stage bicycle race that’s currently underway, is also due to end on Sunday.

“We hope the haze will clear up with recent rains as there are three major events this weekend,” Malaysia’s Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said in a statement. “As of now, they will proceed.”

The organisers of the F1 event and Sepang International Circuit didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Last weekend, poor air quality prompted organisers to shorten a half marathon in Singapore at the last minute. The city-state is due to host an F1 race after the Malaysian event, starting Oct 9. Organisers of the Singapore Grand Prix didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

See also: SIIA report warns of ‘high’ risk from transboundary haze, hints at potential multi-billion dollar economic losses

“Singapore’s air quality will vary day to day depending on wind direction and local showers, but at this stage, there is no clear sign of a sustained pattern change that would quickly end the haze,” said Fergus Keatinge, founder and director of WeatherMapping.com.

Transboundary haze is a near-annual problem in Southeast Asia, but this season is the worst in years as a powerful El Niño brings abnormally hot and dry conditions to Indonesia, fanning wildfires stemming from slash-and-burn land clearing and complicating efforts to bring the blazes under control.

See also: Singapore offers Indonesia help to combat 'scourge' of haze

Rainfall across the archipelago since June has been about 80% below normal, and wet-season rains that usually help extinguish the fires are expected to arrive late this year, according to meteorologists.

The Indonesian Forestry Ministry’s fire-monitoring platform has recorded 15,461 hotspots this month, exceeding levels seen in 2019 and second only to 2015. The fire weather index, a measure of conditions that influence the risk and behaviour of fires, remains very high across large parts of Kalimantan and southern Sumatra, according to the country’s weather agency.

In 2015, another strong El Niño year, haze from Indonesia’s catastrophic fires caused school cancellations, flight diversions and diplomatic tensions across the region. Singapore enacted the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act a year earlier, allowing it to fine companies that cause or condone fires as much as $100,000 a day, though enforcement has proved challenging.

As of early Wednesday, four of Singapore’s five regions recorded “unhealthy” levels of air pollution, according to the National Environment Agency. In its latest outlook, the agency said the “hotspot and smoke haze situation may improve in areas experiencing showers but also continue to stay elevated in areas experiencing prolonged periods of dry weather”.

title: EU member states back move to curb pesticide use in imports
article:
(Sept 30): European Union countries agreed on their stance on rules that will allow the bloc to ban the use of prohibited pesticides in imports from third countries, overcoming a key hurdle for a regulation that has angered major trading partners.

The position reached by the EU’s 27 member states was published in a statement on Wednesday. It slightly broadens the original December proposal from the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, as part of efforts to simplify legislation on food and feed safety.

The rules would give the EU the power to ban imports with traces of pesticides that aren’t authorised in the bloc by setting their so-called Maximum Residue Levels, or MRLs, to zero. It extends the scope of substances covered to also include those that pose risks to bees or groundwater.
